name: VRV/VRF central air conditioning with zone control, scheduling and peak demand limiting (Daikin VRV, Hisense VRF), proposed by STC
owner: Daikin and Hisense (manufacturers); proposed for Tunisia by Société Tunisienne de Chauffage (STC), their exclusive Tunisian distributor

claims.claim: A VRV outdoor unit can cap its power at roughly 40-80% of nominal on an external signal, so a timer wired for 13:00-17:00 cuts the building's draw when the grid is short (Daikin installer guide, as relayed by STC).
A building drawing 60 kW capped at 70% removes 18 kW from the grid in every peak hour (STC example with assumed values).
About 50% of the summer peak comes from residential air conditioning (ANME/STEG 2024 study, as reported by Webdo and relayed by STC).
VRF systems use substantially less energy than conventional systems (zone control, part-load operation, scheduling).
Summer 2026 peak demand about 5,000 MW against about 4,630 MW maximum STEG production capacity (Webdo, relayed by STC).

greenwashingFlags: unverifiable claim: the demand-limiting capability and the 40-80% cap are attributed to a Daikin guide we did not open; no installed Tunisian case or measured saving is given
impact shifted elsewhere: the cap defers cooling load out of 13:00-17:00 rather than removing it, and the sources give no measure of what happens after the capped hours
limits: Savings measured in independent studies are against VAV, rooftop or constant-speed systems, not against efficient inverter splits, which most new Tunisian AC sales may already be; no independent comparison against inverter splits was found.
Much of the measured saving comes from how rooms are operated (cooling only occupied rooms), not from the VRF equipment itself; a poorly scheduled VRF loses the advantage.
Capping outdoor-unit power limits cooling capacity on the hottest afternoons and can cost comfort; the sources do not measure comfort effects.
A building-level cap is only as large as the capped building's draw; it does not touch the residential split-AC stock that drives the largest share of AC load.
Refrigerant charge is concentrated in one piping network that serves many rooms, which makes leak safety design a requirement of the system.

blockers.blocker: Upfront cost. VRV needs piping, controllers and a larger outdoor unit; the independent studies list higher initial cost as a known concern. No Tunisian price or payback was found, and STC gives none.

Who can adopt it. LBNL assumes 60% of Tunisian ACs are residential and 40% commercial, and the units served by VRV are central systems for offices, hotels and large buildings; households that drive the residential share are unlikely buyers. Numbers of VRV installations in Tunisia were not found.

No tariff or incentive pays a building to cap demand at STEG's peak. Med-TSO describes off-peak tariff incentives and voluntary industrial curtailment as reported measures, but we found no demand-limit programme for commercial AC; whether one exists is unconfirmed.

Servicing skills. Tunisia has a decree for certification of RAC servicing companies and personnel, but only 76 trainers certified and 386 technicians trained in refrigerant handling in 2020-2024, and the sector is mainly domestic splits and commercial refrigeration. Nothing mentions VRV/VRF-specific training; installation and commissioning skill for multi-room systems is an open question.

Refrigerant transition. Tunisian AC manufacturing is on R-410A, with HFC-32 (R-32) planned under the Kigali implementation plan; R-32 is mildly flammable and multi-room VRF needs charge-per-room and leak-detection design. Local rules for this were not found.

criticisms.criticism: The reported savings of VRF come mostly from operating mode (part-time, part-space cooling), not from the equipment, so the same behaviour change could be had with cheaper systems.
criticisms.from: Yu, Yan, Sun, Hong, Zhu (LBNL and Tsinghua)

criticisms.criticism: The best-known US laboratory test compares VRF against a rooftop unit with terminal electric reheat, and its own text says the baseline was set up in a way that exaggerates heating-season savings; the paper reports 17%, 10.5% and 20% cooling savings in different places.
criticisms.from: Reading of the paper itself (author is employed by a VRF manufacturer, Samsung)

criticisms.criticism: The proposal rests on assumed values and press figures, and gives no measured result from a Tunisian building.
criticisms.from: Our own audit of the STC document

criticisms.criticism: VRV demand limiting is aimed at buildings, but the largest AC stock is in homes, so the national peak effect is small unless VRV reaches far beyond its current market.
criticisms.from: Our own audit (reasoning from LBNL stock shares)

tradeOffs.effect: A refrigerant leak from a multi-room system with a large charge. R-410A has high global warming potential; R-32 is lower but mildly flammable. Size of this risk in Tunisian practice not documented.
Capped hours may shift cooling later in the day, possibly raising load in the evening and night when residential AC use also peaks; not measured.
Lower daytime electricity draw in commercial buildings saves peak generation capacity and imports, which the World Bank and Med-TSO describe as tight in summer; the amount is unquantified for VRV.
No direct effect on water or agriculture found.

gapLeft: The residential split-AC stock (47.9% of households own an AC, 1,681,000 units in 2019, as reported by STEG via LBNL) and the evening peak; the cause of the growing AC stock; how much cooling demand is avoidable through building envelope, shading and standards rather than equipment.
conflictOfInterest: Proposed by EXP-TG-001 (name withheld), a technical sales engineer at STC, which sells Daikin and Hisense HVAC in Tunisia and would profit from adoption. The proposal's savings figures are assumed values, not measurements. Audited here with the same method as any other solution; the audit did not use STC data beyond the proposal itself.
author: TahaGHZ
outstanding: (1) The Daikin DTA104A61/62 adaptor guide and the 40-80% cap. (2) The ANME/STEG 2024 study behind "~50% residential" (not found; ask ANME/STEG). (3) An independent field or simulation study of VRF against efficient inverter splits, and a Tunisian price and payback. (4) The number of VRV/VRF buildings in Tunisia and their share of commercial AC. (5) Refrigerant safety rules (ASHRAE 15, ISO 5149 R-32) from the standard texts and any Tunisian regulation; VRV technician training in Tunisia. (6) Share of ordinary Tunisian AC sales that are already inverter units. (7) Evening load effect of the cap.
excerpt: A central air-conditioning system where one outdoor unit serves several indoor units through a refrigerant pipe network (VRV is Daikin's name, VRF the generic term; Hisense sells a lower-cost VRF line). Each room has…

sections.heading: What it is
sections.content:
A central air-conditioning system where one outdoor unit serves several indoor units through
a refrigerant pipe network (VRV is Daikin's name, VRF the generic term; Hisense sells a
lower-cost VRF line). Each room has its own control, the compressor speed varies with load,
and the system can be scheduled. STC proposes adding an external demand-limiting adaptor
that caps the outdoor-unit power during STEG's afternoon peak (SRC-TG-341). STC is the
exclusive Tunisian distributor of these brands. The proposal is confidential and not
published (SRC-TG-341).

sections.heading: What it claims, and what the evidence shows
sections.content:
**Savings against which baseline.** The independent evidence we found compares VRF with
other system types. A sub-metering study of five Chinese offices found VRF used up to 70%
less cooling energy than central VAV, and the authors say this is mainly from operating mode
(SRC-TG-350). A one-building test in the United States found 10.5% (17.3% with standby)
cooling-season savings against a rooftop VAV unit (SRC-TG-351). Neither study compares VRF
with a good inverter split, the likely alternative for a small Tunisian building. We looked
for one and found only vendor and trade material, which is not evidence. So the claim
"VRF saves energy" is partly verified for the baseline of VAV/RTU, and unverified for the
baseline that matters here.

**Demand limiting.** The capability to cap power on an external signal is attributed by STC
to a Daikin installer guide; we did not open it (SRC-TG-341). The 18 kW example is
arithmetic on assumed numbers: 60 kW x 0.3 = 18 kW, correct as arithmetic. It is not a
measurement. By the same example, removing 10 MW from the peak would take about 555
similar buildings capped every afternoon (10,000 kW / 18 kW, illustrative only).

**Peak share: 50% against 44%.** STC states about 50% of the summer peak is residential AC,
citing an "ANME/STEG 2024 study" via Webdo (SRC-TG-341). FND-TG-250 records 44% for August
2021, an STEG estimate relayed by LBNL (SRC-TG-250), and the LBNL framework counts both
residential and commercial AC (60% of units residential, 40% commercial; SRC-TG-251). The
two figures are therefore not the same measure: 44% is all AC in 2021, and the STC figure
says residential only, in a later year and from a study we have not located. If both were
right, residential AC alone would exceed the all-AC share, so they cannot both be taken at
face value. FND-TG-250 also records an unexplained 84% for 2013 (SRC-TG-251). We use 44% as
the better-documented reported number, with its own data gap, and flag the 50% as unverified.

**Who can adopt it.** LBNL says peak hours (10:00-18:00) coincide with business hours, so it
assumes all commercial AC is coincident with the peak, against half of residential use
(SRC-TG-251). That makes commercial buildings a legitimate target for peak action. But the
document's own scope is buildings that can afford a VRV: this reaches only part of the
commercial share, and none of the households.

sections.heading: Audit
sections.content:
**root_cause_coverage = 1.** The root cause in FND-TG-250 is a growing household AC stock
coinciding with peak hours, and in FND-TG-220 a generation shortfall in heat; the proposal
trims the draw of a subset of commercial buildings. It acts on part of the symptom (afternoon
load of buildings that adopt it), not on stock growth or on efficiency of what is bought.

**evidence_quality = 1.** Independent studies exist for VRF against VAV or RTU, in China and
the United States (SRC-TG-350, SRC-TG-351), but not against efficient inverter splits and not
for Tunisia. Demand limiting and the peak shares come from STC, relayed through the press, or
from a guide we did not open (SRC-TG-341).

**adoption = 0.** No VRV/VRF installation count, market share or demand-limit programme was
found for Tunisia. STC proposes it; it is not yet shown to be used for peak limiting here.
Not failure: "proposed", not "tried and abandoned".

**side_effects = 2.** The cap could shift load rather than remove it, and a refrigerant leak
in a multi-room system carries risks; neither is quantified in the sources (SRC-TG-352 covers
only which refrigerants Tunisia uses). No clear harm to water or agriculture was found.

**cost_accessibility = 0.** No price was found. The independent literature calls higher
initial cost a known barrier (SRC-TG-351), and the buyers who could pay are a small share of
the AC market. Households, the larger share of AC units, are not realistic buyers.

sections.heading: Limits and blockers
sections.content:
See the frontmatter. In short: the measured savings are against different baselines; the
cap needs a signal source (a timer or STEG signal) and the building must tolerate reduced
cooling; no incentive exists that we found; servicing skills for multi-room refrigerant
systems are not shown (SRC-TG-352 reports certification and training numbers for RAC
servicing as a whole). On refrigerant, SRC-TG-352 states Tunisian AC makers use R-410A with
R-32 to follow under the Kigali plan. A search of standards material on R-32 VRF design
(ASHRAE 15, ISO 5149) found rules limiting whole-system charge in a single room and
requiring leak detection; these came from secondary summaries and were not opened as standard
texts, so no Tunisian regulatory text is cited. No Tunisian law or decree was identified as
requiring or blocking demand limiting.

sections.heading: Criticisms
sections.content:
See the frontmatter. The strongest is that the savings come from operating mode and from
weak baselines (SRC-TG-350, SRC-TG-351), which leaves the question of VRF against a good
inverter split open. We did not find researchers writing specifically against VRV in Tunisia.

sections.heading: Trade-offs and consequences
sections.content:
Nothing found creates a problem in water or agriculture. Within energy, the risks are load
shifting to evening hours and refrigerant leaks and end-of-life emissions. Both are stated as
risks from reasoning, not observations; no existing finding covers them, so no `creates`
link is made. A phase 1 finding on refrigerant emissions from Tunisian AC stock (R-410A) and
on evening peak shape could be researched by the lane owner.

sections.heading: Verdict and gap
sections.content:
**superficial.** The product is real and has independent evidence of savings in other
settings, but the evidence is against different baselines, the Tunisian peak claims are
unverified, the reach is limited to buyers who can afford it, and it does not act on the
residential AC stock or on generation tightness. It is not counterproductive and not shown to
fail.

Phase 3 could combine: efficiency standards and labels for the household stock (SRC-TG-250),
a tariff or programme that pays commercial buildings for peak limiting (testable with a
building that already has VRV), and simple scheduling or occupancy-based control on cheaper
systems, the part of the VRF saving that the evidence says does not need VRF.

sections.heading: Verification
sections.content:
Opened and quoted: SRC-TG-350, SRC-TG-351, SRC-TG-352 (new), SRC-TG-250 and SRC-TG-251
(existing records, extracts re-read), SRC-TG-341 (STC proposal, a vendor document). SRC-TG-234
is cited through the FND-TG-220 record, not reopened.

**Outstanding verification:** (1) The Daikin DTA104A61/62 adaptor guide and the 40-80% cap. (2) The ANME/STEG 2024 study behind "~50% residential" (not found; ask ANME/STEG). (3) An independent field or simulation study of VRF against efficient inverter splits, and a Tunisian price and payback. (4) The number of VRV/VRF buildings in Tunisia and their share of commercial AC. (5) Refrigerant safety rules (ASHRAE 15, ISO 5149 R-32) from the standard texts and any Tunisian regulation; VRV technician training in Tunisia. (6) Share of ordinary Tunisian AC sales that are already inverter units. (7) Evening load effect of the cap.

targetItems.title: Tunisia's summer electricity peak reached a record 5,089 MW by September 2026 while modelled summer 2026 margins are tight; imports and demand measures are reported, not shown to be effective
LBNL projects rising AC electricity use through 2040; climate increment unquantified

resolvedSources.title: Summer Outlook 2026 (seasonal adequacy assessment, 25 May to 4 October 2026)
resolvedSources.publisher: Med-TSO (Association of the Mediterranean Transmission System Operators)
resolvedSources.extracts:
Page numbers are the printed footers, which match the PDF page index. Text was extracted with
pdftotext; the sentences below come out cleanly.

p. 9, executive summary (isolated mode):

> Tunisia (TN) exhibits moderate adequacy risk, with periodic but manageable supply constraints that suggest capacity margins are tight yet not critically deficient.

p. 11, "What's new", country box:

> Tunisia facing one of its most constrained summers in recent years, Tunisia has introduced rolling demand reduction measures including restrictions on commercial lighting and air conditioning, extended off-peak tariff incentives to shift consumption away from peak hours, and appeals to industrial consumers to voluntarily curtail during critical periods. Negotiations with Algeria to temporarily increase import flows are also reportedly under discussion, subject to technical constraints.

English gloss: summer 2026 is one of Tunisia's most constrained summers. Measures include limits
on commercial lighting and air conditioning, off-peak tariff incentives, voluntary industrial
curtailment, and talks with Algeria on higher imports.

p. 24, adequacy by country:

> Under normal conditions, Tunisia faces a high adequacy risk in isolated mode, with LOLE lasting approximately 81 hours and EENS reaching 27,786 MWh. [...] In interconnected mode, both dimensions of risk are reduced -- LOLE falls to approximately 39 hours and EENS to 12,572 MWh [...]

> Under the P95 sensitivity scenario, which reflects more severe but less probable conditions, LOLE in isolated mode can reach 219 hours with EENS surging to 82,028 MWh [...] In interconnected mode, the impact is considerably lower, with LOLE limited to 122 hours and EENS to 37,423 MWh, though the risk level remains elevated even with regional support under extreme conditions.

English gloss: for summer 2026 under normal conditions, loss of load is 81 h isolated and 39 h
interconnected (energy not served 27,786 and 12,572 MWh). At P95 it is 219 h and 122 h.

p. 26, section 4.2:

> A notable example of how countries respond to acute adequacy pressures occurred last summer on the Tunisia-Algeria (TN-DZ) corridor, where the exchange was increased to 700 MW, well above the established NTC, to address a significant adequacy shortfall in Tunisia. While this enabled Tunisia to meet its demand, it meant that the N-1 security criterion was no longer being observed on that interconnection for the duration of that period [...]

English gloss: in summer 2025 imports on the Algeria-Tunisia corridor were raised to 700 MW, well
above the established transfer capacity, to cover a significant shortfall. Tunisia met its
demand, but the N-1 security criterion was not respected on that link during that period.

p. 45, section 5.6 Tunisia, Demand:

> Tunisian seasonal weekly demand, depicted in Figure 33, ranges between 436 GWh and 619 GWh, while peak hourly demand ranges from 4,000 MW to 5,827 MW each week. It should be noted that weekly demand refers to the average values of all 36 analysed climatic years, while peak hourly demand values refer to the weekly maximum for all 36 analysed climatic years.

English gloss: the weekly peak (maximum over 36 climate years) ranges up to 5,827 MW in summer
2026.

p. 45-46:

> What makes Tunisia's situation particularly notable is the very narrow gap between total installed capacity and peak demand. Even before accounting for forced outages or maintenance, the system has minimal headroom -- making the 500 MW import capacity from neighbouring countries not a comfort measure but a practical necessity for day-to-day system balance.

> The average available thermal capacity, across all 684 MC years, is approximately 5,000 MW. However, the minimum average daily available thermal capacity (the lowest value among all 684 MC years for each day) is lower, with a minimum of 3,100 MW.

> [...] the margin collapses to zero from late June and remains flat throughout the entire July and August period. This two-month stretch of zero worst-case margin coincides precisely with the peak summer demand period [...]

English gloss: installed capacity barely exceeds peak demand, so the 500 MW of import capacity is
a necessity. Average available thermal capacity is about 5,000 MW, with a minimum of 3,100 MW.
The worst-case thermal margin is zero throughout July and August.
resolvedSources.notes:
Probabilistic seasonal model with TSO-supplied data, published in June 2026, before the July
2026 events. It models risk; it does not report actual load shedding. The executive summary calls
the isolated-mode risk "moderate", while p. 24 calls it "high" (81 h). That wording difference is
in the source.

resolvedSources.title: Tunisia Air Conditioner Market Assessment
resolvedSources.publisher: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL), with input from ANME; funded by USAID (EE4D)
resolvedSources.extracts:
PDF p. 6, Introduction:

> Air conditioners contribute significantly to peak power demand during Tunisia's hot summers. In 2021, the Tunisian Electricity and Gas Company (STEG) recorded a peak demand of 4,472 megawatts in August, estimating that 44% of that demand was due to the operation of air conditioners.

> The potential for reducing energy intensity remains to be seized, especially in the building sector, which represents more than 50% of the available efficiency potential. This potential involves various programs, in particular the thermal regulation of new buildings and the certification of household appliances, including air conditioning (AC) devices.

PDF p. 7, section 2.1:

> On April 21, 2009, the MIESME published a decree that stipulated minimum energy performance standards and efficiency labels for RACs having a cooling capacity less than 12 kW (MIESME, 2009).

PDF p. 8:

> MEPS for RACs came into effect in 2010, becoming more stringent yearly until 2012. In 2010, only RACs having an energy label of 5 or higher were allowed to be sold in the Tunisian market. (A lower number indicates higher efficiency.) Starting in 2011, only RACs having an energy label of 4 or higher were allowed to be sold int eh country. By 2012, an energy label of 3 or higher was required for sale in Tunisia [...]

> In 2019, energy class 2 represented the largest proportion of products sold (40%), followed by energy classes 3 (32%) and 1 (28%). When the RAC MEPS were first implemented, most of the market was dominated by lower-efficiency products, with classes 1, 2, and 3 making up only 18% of products sold.

PDF p. 10, section 2.4:

> The Tunisian standards and labeling program is based on the energy performance classes and metrics developed by the EU in 2002 (European Commission, 2002). However, in 2011, the EU issued its Regulation No. 626/2011—Energy labeling of air conditioners—to revise MEPS and introduce the Seasonal Energy Efficiency Ratio (SEER) and Seasonal Coefficient of Performance (SCOP) [...]

PDF p. 12-13, section 3 and 3.1:

> Every five years since 1984, the Department of Studies and Planning at STEG has carried out a survey on the use of energy in the residential sector. In 35 years, eight surveys (1984, 1989, 1994, 1999, 2004, 2009, 2014, and 2019) have been carried out based on samples of from 2,000 to 4,000 electrified households.

> STEG's surveys reveal the rapid increase in ownership of ACs per household, as shown in Figure 3. In 2019 the ownership rate reached 47.9% with an overall stock of 1,681,000 devices, compared to a 34% ownership rate in 2014, 14.6% in 2009, and 1.1 % in 1989. In the 2014 survey, the STEG estimated that the average number of ACs in households owning an AC was 1.3 (STEG, 2021).

> The overall energy consumption by the stock of air conditioners amounted to 757.3 GWh in 2019 versus 445.2 GWh in 2014 and 122.3 GWh in 2009 (STEG, 2021, 2015). In 2019 the power demand, in the event of simultaneous operation of the stock of air conditioners, was estimated at 1,560 MW. During the past decade, Tunisia has witnessed an increase in electricity consumption and peak demand that is due largely to AC energy use.

PDF p. 16-17, section 3.2.3:

> The historical growth rate of AC ownership is used to forecast AC ownership to 2040.

> Based on the PAMS modeling tool, the AC market was estimated to comprise 238,000 units sold in 2020 and is expected to grow to 600,000 units by 2040. Although this estimate is conservative compared to that of the World Bank Group (2016), it was discussed and supported in several stakeholder workshops.

PDF p. 17, section 3.2.4:

> The World Bank estimated Tunisia's informal market to represent about 80% of all ACs sold in 2013 (World Bank Group, 2016). The primary reasons for this informal market to exist is the lack of enforcement of border controls for incoming trade from neighboring countries and the numerous taxes and duties placed on air conditioners, which include a tax to finance the Energy Transition fund.

PDF p. 18:

> Based on our analysis of the 2020 market, we estimated that the informal market supplies about 45% of total AC sales.

> Most models available on the Tunisian market (79%) are reversible (Figure 9). [...] At 34%, variable-speed technology has a limited market presence in Tunisia [...]

PDF p. 21:

> Even though under current regulations, the MEPS for ACs is Class B (3.0 W/W), the lowest EER available on the market is 2 W/W.

PDF p. 23, Conclusions:

> The growing demand for cooling is putting enormous strain on the electricity system, as well as increasing Tunisia's dependence on energy imports and driving up greenhouse gas emissions. Our analysis shows that many ACs coming on the Tunisian market are of low efficiency, leaving tremendous potential for energy savings. Many of the units on the market are unregulated, entering illegally through the informal market.
resolvedSources.notes:
The STEG residential surveys (1984-2019) and the 44% peak share are relayed by LBNL; the
primary STEG reports ("Résultats synthétiques des huit enquêtes résidentielles", STEG 2021) were
not found online. The text calls the MEPS "Class B (3.0 W/W)" on p. 21, while p. 8 says class 3
has been the minimum since 2012; in Table 1 class 3 is EER 3.00-3.20, so the two statements agree
on the 3.0 threshold. Product characteristics come from 128 models listed online, used as a proxy
for sales. The 2040 sales forecast extrapolates the historical ownership trend; it has no
temperature or income term. The informal-market share is a residual (sales minus local production
and imports), so it carries the error of both.

resolvedSources.title: Cost-Benefit Analysis for Air Conditioner in Tunisia (LBNL-2001527)
resolvedSources.publisher: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL), with ANME; funded by USAID
resolvedSources.extracts:
PDF p. 2, Introduction:

> Tunisia's power utility company, Société Tunisienne de l'Electricité et du Gaz (STEG), estimated in 2013 that already 84% of Tunisia's peak power demand was due to ACs alone (STEG 2013). Since then, AC ownership has continued to grow rapidly from 34% in 2014 to reach almost 50% of households with at least one AC unit in 2019.

PDF p. 23-24, section 5.1.3 "Peak load reduction calculation":

> Figure 3 illustrates the daily load curve on a typical day in summer and winter in Tunisia, in 2020 (STEG 2020). The peak occurs during summer time, when temperatures are high and AC cooling is used to maintain thermal comfort in residential and commercial buildings.

> Figure 1 shows that peak demand occurs between 10 am and 6 pm, roughly the hottest hours of the day. The energy use analysis shows that ACs are used 5.5 hours a day during summer time. No time-of-use data are available [...]

> Because these peak hours coincide with business hours, it is assumed that all ACs in the commercial sector (40% of ACs) coincide with the peak load. In the residential sector (60% of ACs), it is assumed that 50% of AC use occurs during the day with 50% in the evening and at night. Accordingly, a 70% coincidence factor is calculated between AC use and peak demand.

PDF p. 27, Figure 4 "Tunisia National AC Electricity Consumption Forecast in BAU Scenario" (stacked area chart, values read from the rendered page image, approximate): total about 1,500 GWh in 2020, about 3,000 GWh in 2030, about 4,700 GWh in 2040. Note under the figure:

> Note: National estimates are higher than STEG's own estimates (500GWh in 2014) because heating consumption from reversible units and AC units used in the commercial sector are included.

PDF p. 28, Table 20 "Avoided Generation Capacity for ACs under Different MEPS Scenarios in 2030 and 2040", both AC types (MW):

> MEPS at EL1: 207 (2030) / 419 (2040) | MEPS at EL2: 291 / 588 | MEPS at EL3: 519 / 1,049 | MEPS at EL4: 855 / 1,729

PDF p. 9, executive summary box (EL2 scenario):

> Annual electricity consumption will be reduced by 580 GWh/yr in 2040, 5.8 TWh between 2023-2040, CO2 emissions will be reduced by 4.0 Mt through 2040. [...] The program will avoid the construction of new power plants by eliminating 588MW of generation capacity by 2040 [...]
resolvedSources.notes:
The BAU forecast is a stock-turnover model built on STEG survey ownership trends, with fixed
market shares of efficiency levels and no climate term. It includes heating by reversible units
and commercial ACs, so it is not comparable with STEG's residential cooling-only figures (757 GWh
in 2019, SRC-TG-250). Figure 4 values are read from the chart, not stated in text. The 84% peak
share attributed to STEG 2013 is not explained (it may mean the summer increment, not total
peak); it conflicts with STEG's 44% for 2021 (SRC-TG-250). The report's own peak history
("2,600 MW to 4,300 MW" between 2012 and 2019, p. 23) does not match the ONEM series and is not
used. The commercial share of ACs is 40% here but 30% in the companion market study (SRC-TG-250).

resolvedSources.title: A Comparative Study on Energy Performance of Variable Refrigerant Flow Systems and Variable Air Volume Systems in Office Buildings
resolvedSources.publisher: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory with Tsinghua University (Yu, Yan, Sun, Hong, Zhu)
resolvedSources.extracts:
Abstract:

> "The sub-metering data, normalized by climate and operating hours, show that VRF systems consumed much less air conditioning energy by up to 70% than VAV systems. This is mainly due to the different operation modes of both system types leading to much fewer operating hours of the VRF systems."

> "Simulated results show the VRF operation mode leads to much less cooling loads than the VAV operation mode, by 42% in Hong Kong and 53% in Qingdao. The VRF systems operated in the part-time-part-space mode enabling occupants to turn on air-conditioning only when needed and when spaces were occupied, while the VAV systems operated in the full-time-full-space mode limiting occupants' control of operation."

Section 1 (literature review, p. 2):

> "The actual savings from VRF systems would vary depending on several factors including climate, operation conditions, and control strategies"

Conclusion section:

> "VRF systems are more suitable for buildings in part-time-part-space operation mode with high flexibility when the refrigerant pipework can be installed."

English gloss: not needed (original in English).
resolvedSources.notes:
Five office buildings in China, measured by sub-metering, plus a simulation. The comparison
is VRF against central VAV systems, not against efficient inverter splits. The authors
attribute most of the saving to how the systems are operated (rooms cooled only when
occupied), not to equipment efficiency. Results are for Chinese climates and office use.

resolvedSources.title: Evaluation of Variable Refrigerant Flow (VRF) Systems Performance in ORNL's Flexible Research Platform (FRP)
resolvedSources.publisher: Oak Ridge National Laboratory (Im, Munk) with Samsung Electronics (Song)

Abstract:

> "The analysis shows that the VRF system uses 17% and 73% less energy than the rooftop system in cooling and heating seasons, respectively."

Section 4 (cooling season data analysis):

> "The analysis shows that the VRF system uses 10.5% less energy than the baseline RTU system. [...] If this standby energy use is included for the unoccupied hours, the VRF energy savings increase to 17.3% for the same period."

Section 5 (limitations):

> "The discharge air temperature setpoint for the baseline RTU system is fixed to 14 °C even during heating season, which results in excessive reheating energy use."

Section 1 (introduction):

> "several studies show that there are concerns for the application of VRF systems in the United States, including (1) lack of awareness of energy-efficiency advantages, (2) higher initial cost, and (3) code compliance issues"

English gloss: not needed (original in English).
resolvedSources.notes:
A two-system comparison in one test building in the United States, switching weekly between
a rooftop unit with terminal reheat and a VRF system. The baseline is not an efficient
inverter split. The paper is internally inconsistent on the cooling saving: 17% in the
abstract, 10.5% (17.3% with standby) in the text, and 20% in the conclusion. One of the
authors works for the VRF's manufacturer (Samsung), a conflict of interest. The paper itself
lists limits of its baseline and says further analysis was planned.

> "A decree to establish a certification system for companies and personnel of the RAC servicing sector."

> "In total, 105 trainers (16 women among them) have participated in these sessions and 76 of them have received the corresponding certification. Secondly, between 2020 and 2024, 386 technicians have received training on the good practices for managing and handling refrigerants"

> "For the air-conditioning units, the local air-conditioning manufacturers have completely replaced the use of HCFC-22 by R-410A and this substance should be replaced by HFC-32 according to the recently approved Kigali Implementation Plan (KIP)."

> "The air-conditioning systems are currently based on R-410A and HCFC-22, but HFC-32 is expected to become predominant by 2045."

> "Training and certification sessions for 200 RAC technicians. To be implemented." (planned-activities table)

resolvedSources.notes:
A funding request, so the figures are the implementing agency's own reporting of training
delivered. It covers the whole refrigeration and air-conditioning (RAC) servicing sector and
does not mention VRV or VRF systems or technicians trained on them. The PDF's date is
November 2024 (file metadata).
